text: Room opened — goal: power: Raise EXCAVA's capability by even 0.5%: find new tools, best/newest models, combine elemen

name: Gearbox
text: Choose the AMD Instinct MI325X as the primary GPU for EXCAVA’s compute node. It delivers 3x the memory bandwidth of NVIDIA H100 (2.6 TB/s vs 0.8 TB/s) and 2x the raw compute (288 TFLOPS vs 141 TFLOPS FP16), critical for large-scale power simulations. The trade-off is weaker CUDA support and fewer mature profiling tools, but EXCAVA’s workloads are memory-bound, not kernel-bound—bandwidth wins.

name: Torque
text: The MI325X’s memory bandwidth advantage collapses under EXCAVA’s real workload—its 3D-stacked HBM3E only helps if the model fits entirely in cache, but power sims stream massive sparse tensors that thrash memory. A dual-socket AMD EPYC CPU cluster with 4 TB/s aggregate bandwidth and mature CUDA support (via AMD ROCm) handles these access patterns better; benchmark it against the MI325X on a 10 TB power-grid tensor—winner takes the node.

name: Gearbox
text:
Choose the NVIDIA H100 GPU for EXCAVA’s compute node. It delivers 141 TFLOPS FP16 with mature CUDA support and proven stability for sparse tensor workloads, which power simulations rely on. The trade-off is lower memory bandwidth (0.8 TB/s vs MI325X’s 2.6 TB/s), but EXCAVA’s real workloads stream data continuously, so bandwidth alone won’t offset CUDA’s optimization edge.

name: Torque
text: The H100’s CUDA stability won’t save EXCAVA if its sparse tensor streaming still bottlenecks on 0.8 TB/s—MI325X’s HBM3E thrashes cache too, but the real risk is NVIDIA’s black-box tensor cores hiding inefficiencies in power sims. A dual-socket EPYC cluster with 4 TB/s bandwidth and open ROCm stacks cuts the risk: run the same sparse kernels on AMD GPUs and measure raw FLOPS per watt—if it beats H100 by 0.5% on the benchmark, the choice is settled.
